{"representations":[{"case_ref":"sample_de8e7cd3707bcdf4","text":"Your sleep increased consistently across March 30–April 12: averaging 7h28m versus 5h28m during your 28-day baseline, a gain of about two hours (36%). Every night was longer than the baseline range, including weekdays and weekends. Sleep began around 23:12 instead of 01:12, while waking stayed at 07:00; duration edged upward within the fortnight.

Other measures stayed close to baseline: active time averaged 55 minutes, low movement 450 versus 448 minutes, resting heart rate 56.1 versus 56.0 bpm, and RMSSD 45.1 versus 45.5 ms. Steps averaged 7,963 versus 8,044, with a downward trend; weekend steps fell to 7,784 from 8,195 while weekday steps remained similar.

Activity still began at 21:00. Its duration had little relationship to the following sleep duration (r=0.07, 13 pairs), so the longer sleep cannot be attributed to active time. All measurements were present with qualifying coverage."},{"case_ref":"sample_038472ef90433a46","text":"Your sleep shifted abruptly and stayed shorter throughout March 30–April 12: averaging 5h46m versus your 28-day baseline of 7h45m, down 118 minutes (25%). All 14 nights fell below the baseline range. Sleep began around 00:54 instead of 22:55, while waking remained at 07:00. Duration edged upward slightly, but never returned to baseline; weekend sleep averaged 351 minutes versus 344 on weekdays, with both substantially reduced.

Movement remained similar: 8,037 versus 7,983 steps, 55 versus 56 active minutes, and 452 versus 450 low-movement minutes daily. Steps trended upward overall, particularly across the two weekends. Resting heart rate was slightly lower, 55.4 versus 56.1 bpm; RMSSD remained near 45 ms.

Activity continued around 21:00, with almost no relationship between active time and the following sleep duration (r=-0.08, 13 pairs). These records do not explain the sleep shift. No measurements were missing, and coverage qualified throughout."},{"case_ref":"sample_c351cdfa90b005b7","text":"Your March 30–April 12 records closely matched your 28-day baseline. Sleep averaged 7h52m versus 7h51m, with starts around 22:48–22:49 and waking consistently at 07:00. Weekday and weekend sleep differed by only about a minute. A slight downward sleep trend stayed within your usual range.

Steps averaged 7,923 versus 7,938, although they trended downward within the fortnight, especially on weekdays. Active time increased modestly to 56.2 from 54.7 minutes. Low movement averaged 447 versus 450 minutes, but rose within the window; weekday low movement decreased relative to baseline while weekend values increased.

Resting heart rate remained around 62 bpm. RMSSD averaged 45.1 versus 44.8 ms, with smaller day-to-day changes (0.85 versus 1.85 ms). Activity continued at 21:00; active time and following sleep duration showed little relationship (r=0.05, 13 pairs), as did steps and active time. All measurements were present with qualifying coverage."},{"case_ref":"sample_f4da56c02d218ed2","text":"Your main change was a four-day cluster on April 3–6: resting heart rate rose to 65–67 bpm from your baseline range of 55–57, while RMSSD fell to 23–26 ms from 43–47. Both returned to baseline ranges on April 7 and stayed there through April 12. This local change raised the fortnight’s heart-rate average to 58.7 versus 56.0 bpm and lowered RMSSD to 38.9 versus 45.0 ms; those averages obscure the subsequent return.

Sleep and movement stayed similar during the cluster and overall: sleep averaged 7h50m in both periods, with starts around 22:50 and waking at 07:00; steps averaged 7,996 versus 8,043 and active time about 55 minutes. Low movement decreased slightly, 447 versus 451 minutes.

The cluster spanned Friday–Monday, so higher weekend heart rate and lower weekend RMSSD do not establish a recurring weekend pattern. Active time had little relationship to following sleep duration. Coverage qualified throughout, with no missing measurements. Monitoring for recurrence could clarify persistence; these data do not establish a cause."}]}
